Hi Robert,

Thanks for your comments. I agree that some points in the front-end of 
the paper needed revision. Meanwhile we have corrected these problems in 
a revised version that is now available on arXiv.org. The revised paper 
has a much more thorough theoretical comparison that makes some of your 
comments obsolete.

However, the points you are raising merely affect the theory part of the 
paper. I believe the main point we are making with the analysis is a 
very valid and important one: the TERGM seems to out-perform the SAOM 
across a range of applications where the SAOM's updating process is not 
compatible with the data-generating process. The out-of-sample technique 
we are presenting in the paper will allow users to check if that's the 
case and which model fits better in a given application.

Best regards

Philip

messages.body_plain:
I would say this is a pretty general question that applies equally to 
network modeling and any kind of regression modeling. Unless you are 
obsessed with prediction and don't care about theory, the choice of your 
model terms should be primarily theoretically informed. That said, there 
is one caveat here: if your theory (and especially the endogenous part 
of it) does not fit very well, you may encounter model degeneracy, which 
may prevent you from estimating the model in the first place. So in 
practice it is a mix of theoretical specification and inductive tweaks 
to your theory because it's relatively hard to come up with the perfect 
specification from scratch (if it were possible, we wouldn't need any 
goodness-of-fit measures, after all, because we would know the result 
from the outset). The way I understand your question, though, is that 
you are looking for an algorithm that tries all combinations of model 
terms and reports the one with the best AIC or BIC (i.e., something like 
a stepping algorithm). If that's what you are intending, I think this 
will be neither sensible as it is not theoretically informed (unless you 
do machine learning), nor will it be practical because degeneracy issues 
will not allow you to estimate most model configurations. At least when 
you use MCMC-MLE estimation. If your question is rather about good ways 
to come up with a network theory for a given phenomenon, I would suggest 
reading up on the literature that applies ERGMs and see how they do it. 
The statnet tutorials on the wiki also contain some nice examples.

Best,

Philip

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Franziska -

There's not a standard built-in for that, but there are various 
approaches that might work for you.  The most natural would be to 
compute distances between vertices on your attribute(s) of interest, and 
the use a scaling of a linear combination of that and the geodesic 
distances among vertices to define your coordinates. Here's an ad hoc 
example:

library(sna)
library(network)
data(emon)
s<-emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"  #This is a categorical variable, BTW
s.dist<-outer(s,s,"!=")                  #Get distances with respect to s
g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(emon[[5]]))$gd  #Get geodesic distances
library(MASS)                                 #Needed for non-metric MDS
coord<-sammon(g.dist+0.5*s.dist)$points  #Weight the graph more heavily
plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",coord=coord)

You will note that the vertices with similar sponsorship are now 
co-located.  Adjusting the relative weights of the geodesic distances 
and the attributes will let you tune the importance of each factor in 
the final solution.

A simple function generalizing this can be used to automate the process:

#Demonstration layout function for plot.network that combines attribute 
value scaling and
#scaling by geodesic distances.  layout.par arguments are as follows:
#
#  categorical - Vector of categorical vertex attributes (one value per 
vertex)
#  numeric - Vector or matrix of numeric attributes (one value or row 
per vertex)
#  weights - Numeric vector of length 2 with weights to be used for 
geodesic distances
#    and attribute distances (respectively) in the final solution
#
#Within network, this can be selected by adding mode="geoandattrdist" to 
your plot
#call; note that layout.par=list(...) must be used to specify attributes.)
#
network.layout.geoandattrdist<-function(nw, layout.par){
   require(sna)
   require(MASS)
   g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(nw))$gd          #Get geodesic distances
   g.dist[!is.finite(g.dist)]<-network.size(nw)   #Substitute a large 
value for Inf
   cat.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw)) #Categorical 
distances
   num.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw))  #Numeric distances
   if(!is.null(layout.par$categorical)){                 #Categorical 
attribute
     at<-layout.par$categorical
     cat.dist<-outer(at,at,"!=")
   }
   if(!is.null(layout.par$numeric)){                     #Numeric attribute
     at<-layout.par$numeric
     num.dist<-as.matrix(dist(at))
   }
   at.dist<-cat.dist+num.dist #Attribute distances
   if(is.null(layout.par$weights))                        #Get weights
     weights<-c(1,0.2*max(g.dist)/max(at.dist))
   else
     weights<-rep(layout.par$weights,length=2)
    #Scale the combination of distances and return
coord<-sammon(weights[1]*g.dist+weights[2]*at.dist)$points
    coord
}

Once this is defined, we can easily use it, like so:

plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
   layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"))

plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
   layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location"))

Here's a more complex example (using two dimensions at once, which the 
above code supports for numeric attributes)

crs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Command.Rank.Score"
crs[is.na(crs)]<-0 #Orgs w/NA weren't in the initial response
drs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Decision.Rank.Score"
drs[is.na(drs)]<-0
plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
   layout.par=list(numeric=cbind(crs,drs), weights=c(1,0.1)))

We can also combine numeric and categorical attributes, albeit crudely:

plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location",numeric=cbind(crs,drs)/7, 
weights=c(1,0.5)))

Many more such strategies are possible, but hopefully this provides some 
useful ideas!

-Carter

Your second model is overspecified.  Since you have a maximum degree of

degree(1:5).  The edges term is the sum of all the degree terms, so you 
can't put the whole sequence in the model along with the edges term. 
They're co-linear.

> co-located.  Adjusting the relative weights of the geodesic distances and
> the attributes will let you tune the importance of each factor in the final
> solution.

> geodesic distances
> #    and attribute distances (respectively) in the final solution

>   require(MASS)

> attribute

messages.body_plain:
Yes, that's correct: in this example, the attribute component of the 
layout will be driven by the Euclidean distance between vertices in the 
two dimensional (crs,drs) space.  If you wanted crs vs. drs, you'd want 
to use something like e.g. crs-drs as your numeric attribute.  And 
setting the second weight parameter to a very small value (including 0) 
should give you layout based only on the network.  (Setting the first 
parameter to 0 will similarly give you a layout that depends only on 
attributes.)

Hope that helps!

-Carter

>     Hi, Franziska -
>
>     There's not a standard built-in for that, but there are various
>     approaches that might work for you.  The most natural would be to
>     compute distances between vertices on your attribute(s) of
>     interest, and the use a scaling of a linear combination of that
>     and the geodesic distances among vertices to define your
>     coordinates. Here's an ad hoc example:
>
>     library(sna)
>     library(network)
>     data(emon)
>     s<-emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"  #This is a categorical variable, BTW
>     s.dist<-outer(s,s,"!=")                  #Get distances with
>     respect to s
>     g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(emon[[5]]))$gd #Get geodesic distances
>     library(MASS) #Needed for non-metric MDS
>     coord<-sammon(g.dist+0.5*s.dist)$points #Weight the graph more heavily
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",coord=coord)
>
>     You will note that the vertices with similar sponsorship are now
>     co-located.  Adjusting the relative weights of the geodesic
>     distances and the attributes will let you tune the importance of
>     each factor in the final solution.
>
>     A simple function generalizing this can be used to automate the
>     process:
>
>     #Demonstration layout function for plot.network that combines
>     attribute value scaling and
>     #scaling by geodesic distances.  layout.par arguments are as follows:
>     #
>     #  categorical - Vector of categorical vertex attributes (one
>     value per vertex)
>     #  numeric - Vector or matrix of numeric attributes (one value or
>     row per vertex)
>     #  weights - Numeric vector of length 2 with weights to be used
>     for geodesic distances
>     #    and attribute distances (respectively) in the final solution
>     #
>     #Within network, this can be selected by adding
>     mode="geoandattrdist" to your plot
>     #call; note that layout.par=list(...) must be used to specify
>     attributes.)
>     #
>     network.layout.geoandattrdist<-function(nw, layout.par){
>       require(sna)
>       require(MASS)
>       g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(nw))$gd #Get geodesic distances
>     g.dist[!is.finite(g.dist)]<-network.size(nw) #Substitute a large
>     value for Inf
>     cat.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw)) #Categorical
>     distances
>     num.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw)) #Numeric
>     distances
>       if(!is.null(layout.par$categorical)){         #Categorical attribute
>         at<-layout.par$categorical
>         cat.dist<-outer(at,at,"!=")
>       }
>     if(!is.null(layout.par$numeric)){ #Numeric attribute
>         at<-layout.par$numeric
>         num.dist<-as.matrix(dist(at))
>       }
>       at.dist<-cat.dist+num.dist                           #Attribute
>     distances
>     if(is.null(layout.par$weights)) #Get weights
>     weights<-c(1,0.2*max(g.dist)/max(at.dist))
>       else
>         weights<-rep(layout.par$weights,length=2)
>        #Scale the combination of distances and return
>     coord<-sammon(weights[1]*g.dist+weights[2]*at.dist)$points
>        coord
>     }
>
>     Once this is defined, we can easily use it, like so:
>
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
>     layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"))
>
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
>     layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location"))
>
>     Here's a more complex example (using two dimensions at once, which
>     the above code supports for numeric attributes)
>
>     crs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Command.Rank.Score"
>     crs[is.na <http://is.na>(crs)]<-0 #Orgs w/NA weren't in the
>     initial response
>     drs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Decision.Rank.Score"
>     drs[is.na <http://is.na>(drs)]<-0
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
>       layout.par=list(numeric=cbind(crs,drs), weights=c(1,0.1)))
>
>     We can also combine numeric and categorical attributes, albeit
>     crudely:
>
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
>     layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location",numeric=cbind(crs,drs)/7,
>     weights=c(1,0.5)))
>
>
> plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist", 
> label=emon[[5]]%v%"Decision.Rank.Score", label.pos=5,
>      edge.col="grey", layout.par=list(numeric=cbind(crs,drs), 
> weights=c(1,0.000001))) # weight on network
>
>
>     Many more such strategies are possible, but hopefully this
>     provides some useful ideas!
>
>     -Carter

   theory, if there is a shared partner in the undirected wars network (e.g.
   A-C and B-C at war), it will reduce the likelihood of a threat A -> B or B

Jeff Carnegie

messages.body_plain:
Ya,

I'm guessing you're trying to fit a model that has too many parameters 
for the little data you have available, and your data collection forces a 
constraint that max(degree)=5 that needs to be included.

I'd suggest you try fitting the degree constraint with 
constraints=~bd(maxout=5) (see ?"ergm-constraints"), and then dropping 
the degree terms.

Then try starting with simpler models (nodefactor terms only), and 
adding the nodematch terms, each one separately, with diff=F (the 
default), before putting them all in together.

But the bottom line here is that you have very little data, so you may not 
be able to identify all the effects of interest.

best,
mm

as.network.nodelist<-function(x,bipartite=FALSE,...){
   x<-as.matrix(x)
   # construct a table of ids
   vertex.names<-unique(as.vector(x))
   vertex.names<-vertex.names[!is.na(vertex.names)]
   if(bipartite){
     # permute so that the first elements appear as events
     vertex.names<-c(x[,1],vertex.names[!vertex.names%in%x[,1]])
     bipartite<-nrow(x)
   }
   rows<-lapply(1:nrow(x),function(r){
     i<-match(x[r,1],vertex.names)
     j<-match(x[r,which(!is.na(x[r,]))[-1]],vertex.names)
     cbind(i,j)
   })
   edgelist<-do.call(rbind,rows)
   net<-network(edgelist,matrix.type='edgelist',bipartite=bipartite,...)
   network.vertex.names(net)<-vertex.names
   return(net)
}
